text.p: International and U.S. envoys condemned comments attributed to indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic on Monday, accusing him of breaking a pledge to stay out of the public arena.
Karadzic, wartime Bosnian Serb leader, was quoted by a Greek newspaper as saying that Serbs would go to war again if the territorial dispute over the town of Brcko was not "solved".

Sunday's Eleftheros Typos quoted Karadzic dismissing the Dayton peace agreement as a mere "ceasefire" and shrugging off his possible arrest to face charges before the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia in the Hague.
A spokesman for the office of the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, called Karadzic's reported comments "an outrageous provocation" which would not be tolerated.

Spokesman Colum Murphy said Karadzic had promised in a July agreement brokered by U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke that he would step down as Bosnian Serb president and refrain from making public statements.
"This is a violation of the agreement reached with the High Representative and Mr Holbrooke," Murphy told reporters.
Provocative rhetoric was risky at a time when the volatile dispute over Brcko was due to be decided by an arbitration panel within two weeks, Murphy said.
"Dr Karadzic has made a major mistake...by such outrageous statements (he) has hastened the day that he will be able to comment only from the Hague."
U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum also castigated Karadzic over his reported threats and said Serb leaders had disowned his comments.
"We have stated immediately that this interview is unacceptable both in its form and its content," Kornblum told reporters during a visit to Sarajevo.
Kornblum said the United States rejected any threats issued by Karadzic and that the presence of NATO-led peacekeeping troops made it impossible for him to carry out such threats.
The American diplomat said he had conveyed Washington's dismay to the Serb member of the collective presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, and the Bosnian Serb president, Biljana Plavsic.
"I am satisfied to say both Krajisnik and Plavsic did not accept the form or the content of this interview."
The Bosnian Serb information ministry issued a statement on Monday saying the interview with Karadzic was "fabricated".

"Since he transferred his powers to Biljana Plavsic on June 30 last year, Dr Radovan Karadzic has not appeared in public nor has he authorised anyone to lay out his stands in public," the statement said.

The ministry said Karadzic had not authorised any statements which would be "contrary to the official Serb position, which is characterised by full commitment to the Dayton agreement and its implementation".

In the past, Karadzic has sought out Greek media to criticise international peace efforts and the work of the U.N. war crimes tribunal. Twice indicted by the tribunal, Karadzic still exerts political influence behind the scenes in Bosnia's Serb entity, diplomats say.
